content: The fossils known as Java Man were discovered in 1891 at Trinil, located on the banks of the Bengawan Solo River in East Java, Indonesia. These fossils represent one of the earliest known specimens of Homo erectus. The discoverer, Eugène Dubois, assigned the scientific name Pithecanthropus erectus to the specimen, a term derived from Greek and Latin roots meaning upright ape-man. Dubois' discovery was not a complete skeleton. It consisted of a skullcap, a femur, and a few teeth. There has been some debate among scientists as to whether all these bones belong to the same species. In 1936, a second, more complete specimen was unearthed in the village of Sangiran, located 18 kilometers north of Solo in Central Java. This find, which included a skullcap of similar size to the one discovered by Dubois, was made by the German-born paleontologist G.H.R. von Koenigswald. Since then, numerous additional fossils have been uncovered at the Sangiran site. However, official evaluations of the site have criticized its inadequate presentation and interpretation of the findings. For a time, the fossils discovered by Dubois and Koenigswald were considered the oldest hominid remains ever found, until older human fossils were unearthed in the Great Rift Valley in Kenya. Some scientists of the era proposed that Java Man might represent an intermediate evolutionary form between modern humans and the common ancestor shared with other great apes. However, the prevailing view among contemporary anthropologists is that the direct ancestors of modern humans were African populations of Homo erectus (or possibly Homo ergaster), rather than the Asian populations represented by Java Man and Peking Man. As with many significant hominid fossil discoveries, Java Man has been the subject of controversy, particularly among creationists. Some creationists have sought to diminish the evolutionary importance of Java Man by arguing that the specimen should be classified as either fully human or fully ape. For example, one argument claims that Java Man is a true member of the human family, while another, incorrect claim suggests that Dubois himself later concluded that Java Man was actually a large gibbon.
